title: Six students per professor, in algebra
hook: One sentence, three equations. Which one says what the sentence says?

knows: reading and evaluating an expression like 6 × P
doesNotKnow: how to turn a "times as many" sentence into an equation
that letters stand for numbers of things, not for the things

misconception: "Six times as many students as professors" is written 6S = P, reading the letters as labels ("6 students, 1 professor").
objective: The learner can explain that S = 6P is right because S and P are counts: substituting real counts (2 professors, 12 students) makes S = 6P true and 6S = P false, and 6S = P would mean six professors per student.

claims.text: With P professors each having 6 students, S = 6P reads S = 6 × P (true), 6S = P reads 6 × S = P (false) and 6S = 6P is false; for example P = 2, S = 12: 12 = 12, 72 = 2 and 72 = 12; P = 4, S = 24: 24 = 24, 144 = 4.
claims.source: Substitute S = 6P: 6P = 6P holds; 6(6P) = 36P ≠ P for P ≥ 1; 6(6P) = 36P ≠ 6P for P ≥ 1. node: [[2,12],[4,24]].map(([P,S])=>[S===6*P,6*S===P,6*S===6*P]) gives [true,false,false] twice. The stage computes S = k × P and prints each side from EQS. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own: P = 2, S = 12: S = 6P '12 = 12' true, 6S = P '72 = 2' false, 6S = 6P '72 = 12' false; P = 4, S = 24: 24 = 24, 144 = 4, 144 = 24. EQS show() prints those sides; S = k x p.

claims.text: "Six times as many students as professors" means S = 6P for every positive number of professors, so it stays true when the number of professors changes.
claims.source: Definition of "a times as many X as Y": X = a × Y. With k = 6 the stage makes S = 6P for P = 1..5. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Definition 'a times as many X as Y' -> X = aY. At k = 6 the stage gives S = 6P for P = 1..5; milestone resize needs two P values at k = 6.

claims.text: For positive counts, 6S = P says there are six professors for every student (professors outnumber students six to one).
claims.source: 6S = P ⇔ P / S = 6 for S > 0. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. 6S = P with S > 0 gives P/S = 6.

claims.text: In these equations the letters S and P stand for counts (numbers of students and professors), not for the people themselves; the multiplier goes on the smaller group: 6 × P gives the number of students.
claims.source: Algebra convention: a variable stands for a number. Follows from c2 (S = 6P, and P < S for P ≥ 1). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Convention; the reveal's 'Multiply the smaller group by 6 to get the bigger one' matches S = 6P with P < S for P >= 1.

claims.text: When there are not 6 students per professor, S = 6P is false (stage: e.g. 4 per professor with P = 2 reads 8 = 12).
claims.source: S = kP = 6P only if k = 6 (P ≥ 1). The k ≠ 6 reveal branch quotes the stage's current values. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. S = kP = 6P only if k = 6; at k = 4, P = 2: '8 = 12', false. The k != 6 reveal branch prints the current values; 'at six per professor it was the only true one' holds (36P != 6P, 36P != P).

recall.question: There are four times as many chairs as tables. C = number of chairs, T = number of tables. Which equation fits?
recall.why: C and T are counts. With 3 tables there are 12 chairs, and C = 4T reads 12 = 12. 4C = T would say tables outnumber chairs.
